Donald Trump Set to Hit India, China & Others With New Tariffs
US President Donald Trump is considering another round of tariff increases on India, China and several other major trading partners, with Beijing expected to face some of the steepest duties, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.
The proposed move follows a months-long investigation by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) into government subsidies and excess industrial production in 16 economies. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer is expected to disclose the findings as early as this week, although the timing of the announcement could change, the report said.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
Washington believes that government support in these countries allows domestic manufacturers to produce goods beyond market demand and sell them at lower prices in international markets. The Trump administration argues that such practices put American manufacturers at a disadvantage and weaken the country's industrial base.
The investigation was initiated in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The provision gives the US administration the authority to take trade action, including imposing additional duties, against countries found to be engaging in unfair trade practices.
Apart from China and India, the investigation covers the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Cambodia, Singapore, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Switzerland, Norway and Mexico.
Greer had earlier said the investigation would examine economies showing signs of structural excess production, including countries with persistent trade surpluses or manufacturing facilities operating below their actual capacity.
China Likely To Face Higher Tariffs
China is expected to be among the countries facing the biggest tariff increases because of the scale of its government support for domestic industries, according to the WSJ report.
The proposed duties could cover a wide range of imported products, although goods such as steel, aluminium and automobiles that are already subject to separate national security tariffs are expected to be excluded.
The final tariff rates have not yet been announced. However, the report suggests that the administration is considering rates broadly aligned with the trade arrangements negotiated with different countries earlier. The European Union, Japan and South Korea could face duties of 15% or lower, while India and Vietnam could be exposed to higher rates.
What The Fresh Tariff Move Means For India
The latest development comes at a crucial time for India, which is negotiating a bilateral trade agreement with the United States.
Earlier this month, a senior Indian government official said Washington had assured New Delhi of a comparative tariff advantage over competing economies under the proposed trade arrangement.
The official said the advantage would depend on the final tariff structure and the outcome of the USTR's ongoing investigations. India is aiming to conclude the first tranche of the bilateral trade agreement by the end of the current financial year, with negotiations on the initial phase and the broader agreement progressing simultaneously.
India has already faced additional US duties under a separate Section 301 investigation concerning restrictions on imports of goods produced using forced labour. In July 2026, the US imposed an additional 10% ad valorem duty on Indian imports under that investigation.
The outcome of the latest probe into excess industrial capacity could therefore become another important factor in determining the future of India-US trade relations.

sources.text:
US President Donald Trump's administration is reportedly preparing to increase tariffs on several countries, including China and India, arguing that their governments have harmed American companies by supporting domestic industrial production. Citing sources, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday (local time) that Jamieson Greer, the US Trade Representative (USTR), is likely to announce the tariffs as soon as this week. The move follows a months-long investigation into industrial subsidies provided by countries including China, the European Union, and 14 other nations. However, sources cautioned that the timeline could change. According to Greer, subsidies and other forms of government support provided to companies in certain countries have created excess industrial capacity in those economies. This allows their firms to flood global markets with cheaper goods, ultimately undermining US producers. While the final tariff rates remain unclear, Trump administration officials have repeatedly said they intend to impose duties similar to those introduced by the US President in 2025, before the Supreme Court struck down his first batch of tariffs in February 2026. The proposed tariff announcement also comes amid a separate controversy involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and allegations that the company's advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips were smuggled into China despite tighter US export restrictions. According to the WSJ, the timing of the tariff move could also be linked to an attempt by the Trump administration to divert attention from questions surrounding what the government knew about the alleged smuggling and its response to the matter. The USTR's announcement is also expected to bring higher tariffs for dozens of countries, including China, Japan, South Korea and the 27 member nations of the European Union. The new duties are likely to cover most products exported from these countries. However, certain industrial goods, including steel, aluminium and automobiles, are expected to be excluded as they are already subject to tariffs under a separate national security provision. Countries that reached trade agreements with the Trump administration, including Japan and the European Union, are expected to retain tariff rates in line with the terms they had agreed to before the Supreme Court's ruling, according to people familiar with the plans. Under this arrangement, the EU, Japan and South Korea could face tariffs of 15% or less, while countries such as Vietnam and India may be subject to higher rates depending on the terms of their respective trade deals with Trump. China, on the other hand, is likely to face higher tariffs than many other countries, as Trump administration officials have pointed to the extensive nature of Beijing's subsidies and their disruptive impact on the global economy. The administration may also introduce provisions allowing it to raise tariffs on countries if their industrial overcapacity increases or they fail to implement policy changes during future trade negotiations with the US, the report added. The proposed tariffs are expected to be imposed on top of duties announced under a separate measure in July. The measure targeted countries that failed to prevent the trade of goods manufactured using forced labour and set tariff rates ranging from 10% to 12.5% across 60 economies. However, the measure is currently facing a legal challenge in court. Earlier in July, the US announced fresh tariffs on several countries under Section 301. While India was initially placed in the 12.5% tariff bracket, it was moved to the 10% category following discussions on labour practices. The development followed the USTR's decision in March to launch investigations into 60 economies under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act of 1974. The probe aimed to determine whether their trade practices were linked to a failure to enforce restrictions on imports of goods manufactured using forced labour. The duties, ranging from 10% to 12.5%, cover several major US trading partners, including India, the UK, the European Union, Canada and Japan. According to the Office of the USTR, "Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting US commerce. sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and 14 other economies, according to two people familiar with the matter.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office is expected to release the results of a monthslong tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies by the 16 economies in the coming days, according to the people who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
They stressed the timing for the rollout of the tariffs could still change. The White House and USTR did not respond to requests for comment.
Plans for the new tariffs are part of an effort to replace broader duties the administration set last year that were subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.
The tariffs are in response to what the White House has said is excessive manufacturing output in those countries, boosted by subsidies, that has led to a flood of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies.
The anticipated action constitutes a second step in the administration’s efforts to replace the duties announced in April 2025 that the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional in February. The White House slapped 60 trading partners with levies of 10% to 12.5% in July, charging that they have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
The anticipated trade action demonstrates that the Trump administration is still willing to impose import taxes despite a sweeping loss for the Republican Party in this month’s midterm elections, fueled largely by affordability concerns as inflation remains elevated. At the same time, the new duties could test how the Democrats will respond to tariffs imposed unilaterally by Trump.
Even with majorities in both the House and Senate, Trump could veto any legislation that overturns or waters down the tariffs.
The excess industrial capacity probes were initiated under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to levy tariffs against nations that discriminate against U.S. companies or commerce.
The levels of the anticipated tariffs were not immediately clear, but would come on top of tariffs of 10% to 12.5% announced earlier this year.
Many countries, including China, had protested those tariffs, which took effect just as the clock ran out on temporary levies Trump had turned to after the Supreme Court in February struck down sweeping “reciprocal” tariffs he levied on nearly every U.S. trade partner.
The expected move comes as Trump just last week visited the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen for his third face-to-face engagement with Chinese President Xi Jinping this year. Xi’s expected to travel to Doral, Florida, next month for the Group of 20 Summit, which Trump is hosting.
While Trump has moved to build a closer relationship with Xi, the yawning trade deficit remains a significant irritant in the U.S.-China relationship.
Massive capacity in a slew of Chinese industries, from autos to solar panels, cement and steel manufacturing, has drawn increased attention from Beijing’s trading partners in recent years.
Although China’s own leaders have prioritized rebalancing the economy, slowing domestic demand has prompted companies to expand into overseas markets. Surging exports pushed China’s trade surplus to a record of nearly $1.2 trillion last year.

sources.news_title: Trump administration set to unveil new tariffs after probe on excess factory capacity: sources
sources.text:
The Trump administration is poised to imminently release the findings of a probe aimed at countering alleged excess industrial capacity in 16 major U.S. trading partners, three people with knowledge of the matter said on Tuesday (November 24, 2026), with new import duties on a wide range of goods expected.
The results of the investigation are expected as soon, these people said. The U.S. Trade Representative’s office is expected to propose ‌new duties that would stack on top of previous tariffs already imposed during President Donald Trump’s second term.
The duties would partly replace tariffs struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court in February. The administration’s tariffs have in part ‌contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the United States, and a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll following November’s midterm elections ‌showed 62% of respondents would support efforts to repeal the tariffs.
Tailored tariff rates
It is unclear what tariff rates would be proposed. One of the people said that the duties would be specifically tailored to each country, with goods from Mexico and Norway unlikely to see any immediate levies.
USTR has been investigating most of the US’s largest trading partners under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 over what it called evidence of excess industrial capacity.
The White House is ‌expected to honor capped tariff rates that were included in finalized US trade deals with partner countries, this person said. These include duty caps of 15% on goods from the EU, Japan and South Korea and 19% for Malaysia.
The U.S. also is expected to honor the 20% cap on Trump’s second-term tariffs on goods from China, as long as a ‌trade truce due to expire on January 10 is extended. If it expires, the Chinese excess capacity rate would rise to a higher level.
The U.S. Trade Representative’s office and the White House did not respond to Reuters queries about the pending announcement.
Ryan Majerus, a former senior Commerce Department trade official, said he expects a lengthy report that could include differentiated tariff remedies for each of the 16 trading partners.
Majerus, a partner with King & Spalding, said the administration could propose high tariff rates of 15% to 25% on imports from countries deemed to have excess capacity in various sectors. ‌Those levies would stack on top of existing tariffs of 10% or 12.5% imposed under a separate investigation into lax enforcement of anti-forced labor laws.
However, he said the administration could also propose lower tariff rates with escalation clauses that would ratchet rates higher over time unless countries take steps to reduce excess production capacity.
Replacement tariffs
The countries included in the probe are China, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia, along with the European Union.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that the probe’s results could be unveiled as soon as this week.
USTR launched the excess capacity probe in March, along ‌with a separate probe into weak or lax enforcement of anti-forced labor laws in 59 countries and the European Union. Together, the duties are meant to rebuild Trump’s global “Liberation Day” tariffs that were struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court in February.
The Trump administration has singled out China as the biggest source of excess industrial capacity, which it says is flooding global markets with steel, aluminum, electric vehicles, appliances, solar products and other goods. China has rejected the accusations, saying its exports reflect competitive advantages.
The probe is also partly directed at Chinese investment into countries in Southeast Asia, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, to manufacture goods for the US market and avoid prior US tariffs.
Under a U.S.-China trade truce due to expire on January ‌10, the Trump administration has capped second-term tariffs on Chinese goods at 20%, in addition to duties of about 25% imposed during Mr. Trump’s first term. The US has already imposed a 12.5% anti-forced labor duty on all Chinese imports, leaving only 7.5% to reach the 20% cap.
The U.S. and China also are working to cut tariffs on $30 billion of non-strategic imports from each side.

USTR has been investigating what it called evidence of excess industrial capacity in most of the US's largest trading partners. They are China, the European Union, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that the probe's results could be unveiled as soon as this week.
The U.S. Trade Representative's office and the White House did not immediately respond to Reuters queries about the pending tariff announcement.
USTR launched the excess capacity probe in March, along with a separate probe into weak or lax enforcement of anti-forced labor laws in 59 countries and the European Union. In July, the Trump administration imposed import duties of 10 percent or 12.5 percent on goods from those 60 trading partners.
It was unclear what tariff rates would be charged on imports, or what exemptions may be granted, the people said. The Trump administration has singled out China as the biggest source of excess industrial capacity, which it says is flooding global markets with steel, aluminum, electric vehicles, appliances, solar products and other goods. The probe is partly directed at Chinese investment into countries in Southeast Asia, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, to manufacture goods for the U.S. market and avoid tariffs.

One of the people said that the 20 percent cap would likely be maintained as long as the trade truce is extended. If it expires, the excess capacity rate would snap to a higher level, providing incentive for Beijing to extend it.

President Donald Trump’s administration is preparing to impose higher tariffs on China, the European Union and other major trading partners following an investigation into foreign government subsidies and industrial policies that U.S. officials contend disadvantage American manufacturers.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could announce the investigation’s findings as early as this week, according to a Tuesday report by The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the administration’s plans. The proposed measures could affect imports from dozens of countries, including China, Japan, South Korea and the European Union’s 27 member states.
The investigation covers China, the European Union and 14 other economies accused of maintaining policies that encourage industrial production beyond domestic demand, potentially allowing subsidized manufacturers to sell goods abroad at prices that American competitors struggle to match.
China could face particularly significant tariff increases because administration officials consider its industrial subsidies among the most extensive and disruptive to international markets. However, the final tariff rates, affected products and implementation dates have not been publicly announced.
According to additional reporting on the administration’s plans, imports from the European Union, Japan and South Korea, currently subject to tariffs ranging from approximately 10% to 12.5%, could face rates approaching 15%. Those potential increases would reflect trade arrangements negotiated during Trump’s second term.
The administration is also reportedly considering provisions allowing tariffs to increase further if foreign governments fail to modify industrial policies or if excess manufacturing capacity continues expanding.
The anticipated announcement follows a broad trade investigation launched in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which authorizes the U.S. trade representative to investigate foreign practices considered unreasonable, discriminatory or harmful to American commerce.
In its March 11 announcement initiating the investigations, the Office of the United States Trade Representative identified China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India as economies subject to examination.
The agency said government intervention in manufacturing sectors can distort global trade by encouraging production that exceeds domestic consumption, creating surpluses that are subsequently exported to international markets.
Greer argued when the investigations began that the United States should not continue accepting the consequences of industrial policies that support foreign production at the expense of American businesses.
“The United States will no longer sacrifice its industrial base to other countries that may be exporting their problems with excess capacity and production to us,” Greer said.
The USTR’s accompanying fact sheet identified several practices under examination, including direct government subsidies, subsidized lending, state-owned enterprises, restrictions on foreign market access, currency policies and government measures supporting production disconnected from normal market demand.
Officials also examined whether weak labor protections, suppressed wages and inadequate environmental standards provide manufacturers in certain countries with competitive advantages over American businesses.
The investigations focused on structural excess capacity in manufacturing, a condition in which factories and industrial facilities can produce substantially more goods than domestic or global markets can absorb at economically sustainable prices.
U.S. officials argue that such conditions can lead foreign manufacturers to increase exports at artificially low prices, potentially contributing to factory closures, reduced investment and job losses in competing American industries.
The administration’s investigation included public hearings beginning May 5 and opportunities for businesses, industry groups and foreign governments to submit comments.
Section 301 permits the United States to impose additional import duties or pursue other trade measures after determining that foreign government practices burden or restrict American commerce.
The latest tariff preparations follow a major legal setback for Trump’s trade agenda earlier this year.
On Feb. 20, the Supreme Court invalidated tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, limiting the administration’s ability to rely on emergency economic authority for broad import duties.
The administration subsequently pursued alternative statutory authorities, including Section 301, to maintain or establish trade restrictions.
Unlike the emergency powers previously invoked by Trump, Section 301 provides a specific legal framework for responding to foreign trade practices following an investigation and formal findings.
The latest initiative could therefore provide a more durable legal basis for tariffs targeting subsidies and industrial policies across multiple countries.
However, additional duties could also complicate negotiations with major American trading partners that have already reached agreements with Washington.
The European Union, Japan and South Korea negotiated trade arrangements with the Trump administration in 2025, establishing tariff frameworks intended to reduce uncertainty and improve market access.
New duties could raise questions about how those agreements would interact with additional trade enforcement measures.
The potential tariffs also come amid renewed efforts by Washington and Beijing to manage their economic relationship.
The United States and China have maintained negotiations involving tariffs, agricultural trade, industrial exports and restrictions on sensitive technologies. Their current trade truce has been extended into January 2027, although officials have not reached a comprehensive longer-term agreement.
Additional tariffs targeting Chinese industrial subsidies could introduce new complications into those discussions, particularly if Beijing responds with restrictions on American exports.
The economic effects would depend on the products covered, the final tariff rates and how businesses adjust their supply chains.
Tariffs are collected from U.S. importers, which may absorb the additional costs, negotiate lower prices with overseas suppliers or pass some expenses along to American businesses and consumers.
Domestic manufacturers competing with subsidized foreign products could benefit from reduced import competition, while American companies relying on imported materials and components could face higher production costs.
The announcement also comes as the administration faces renewed scrutiny over consumer prices following the November midterm elections, which resulted in Democrats gaining control of both chambers of Congress beginning in January.
Although the proposed trade measures are intended to support domestic manufacturing, their effects on consumer prices, business costs and international supply chains remain uncertain.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the timing of Greer’s announcement could change, and the administration has not yet publicly released its final findings or detailed tariff schedule.
If implemented, the measures would represent another significant expansion of Trump’s trade restrictions, shifting attention toward foreign industrial subsidies and manufacturing overcapacity as the administration seeks to protect American industries through additional import duties.

The impact is unlikely to be uniform across all countries. Japan, the European Union and South Korea, which had negotiated trade arrangements with the Trump administration, are expected to face tariffs of 15 per cent or lower, according to people familiar with the plans.
The tariffs on India and Vietnam might be comparatively high due to the conditions of their separate agreements with the US government. However, the tariffs on China are expected to be especially high because the subsidies in China are numerous and highly disruptive, according to the representatives of the Trump administration.
The administration is also considering provisions that could allow Washington to raise duties further if a country's industrial overcapacity increases or if it fails to make policy changes during future negotiations.
WHY THE INDIA-US TRADE DEAL IS STILL ON HOLD
The proposed tariff action could further complicate India's efforts to conclude a trade agreement with the US. The two countries announced an interim trade framework on February 7, 2026. Under the arrangement, Washington had agreed to reduce its reciprocal tariff on Indian goods from 25 per cent to 18 per cent and withdraw another 25 per cent penalty tariff imposed over India's purchases of Russian oil.
However, the agreement ran into uncertainty later that month when the US Supreme Court struck down the reciprocal tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). That ruling forced Washington to reconsider its tariff arrangements and develop a new framework for duties on imports from different countries.
Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal explained on November 18 that India and the US could not formally sign their proposed trade agreement until the new American tariff structure was established. Speaking at a Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) event, Agrawal said the original trade framework had been negotiated against the backdrop of tariffs that were subsequently struck down by the US Supreme Court.
"The challenge that you need to appreciate is that the deal (framework for the first tranche of the bilateral trade agreement) was announced (in February) in the background of executive tariffs that were existing at that point of time. Those tariffs have been struck down by the Supreme Court there. Now a new tariff architecture is being created by the US," Agrawal said.
WHY SECTION 301 PROBE MATTERS FOR INDIA
There is another hurdle beyond the uncertainty surrounding the Supreme Court ruling.
The US is conducting investigations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to examine trade practices it considers unfair and potentially impose additional duties in response. One of these investigations concerns industrial overcapacity and government subsidies. India is among the countries being examined, alongside several competing economies.
The findings could lead to fresh penalties on imports, making the outcome particularly important for countries negotiating trade agreements with Washington.
Agrawal said both sides wanted to conclude the negotiations quickly and that the legal agreement was in its final stages. However, he stressed that India needed clarity on the new US tariff structure and the outcome of the ongoing investigations before signing a deal.
"Until the tariff architecture comes back in place, signing of a deal, I think will take some time," he said.
"Every country will like to have a deal which gives them certainty around all the investigations that are going on. You cannot have a deal till there are uncertainties around multiple investigations that are going on," Agrawal said.
The proposed new duties could also be imposed alongside tariffs announced under a separate US action in July targeting economies that fail to block trade in goods produced using forced labour. That measure established additional tariffs ranging between 10 per cent and 12.5 per cent for a group of 60 economies. However, it is currently facing a legal challenge.

sources.text:
Quick Take
- The Wall Street Journal reported preparations for higher US tariffs on China, the European Union and other trading partners.
- The USTR docket showed no determination, tariff schedule or start date for the manufacturing overcapacity inquiry as of Nov. 24.
- A presidential post can alert markets before formal tariff terms establish which goods are covered, what rates apply and when.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 24 that the US was preparing higher tariffs on China, the European Union, and other trading partners, which could impact Bitcoin.
Citing people familiar with the plans, the Journal reported that US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer could release the findings of a months-long investigation into manufacturing overcapacity as soon as this week.
On Nov. 24, the USTR docket still showed the investigation opened in March and four days of hearings in May, listing no determination or tariff schedule for the case. A check of published USTR notices in the Federal Register found none dated Nov. 19 through Nov. 24.
The available White House, Treasury, and Commerce trade agency listings carried no announcement of the action described in the report. Importers still have no published list of the goods that would face these duties, the rates that would apply or the date they would start.
Where the investigation stands
On Nov. 20, Greer told Bloomberg Television he expected the work to be finished by year-end. He declined to specify which economies might face additional tariffs.
USTR opened the investigations on March 11 under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 and is examining whether policies such as subsidies sustain more manufacturing capacity than demand supports and whether those practices burden or restrict US commerce.
The agency’s fact sheet described the sectors it wanted to examine. An investigation of how a product is made or subsidized leaves open which products, if any, may face duties.
The inquiry covers 16 economies, including the EU. The March 17 initiation notice also lists Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India. Hearings ran from May 5 through May 8.
Under Section 304 of the Trade Act, USTR must determine whether the practices are actionable. If it makes an affirmative finding, it must decide what action, if any, to take. The law requires the trade representative to publish the determination and the facts it rests on in the Federal Register.
On July 23, USTR announced final duties on 60 economies after separate investigations into their failures to impose and enforce bans on imports made with forced labor.
Bitcoin crashed when Trump announced a tariff change
On April 9, 2025, President Donald Trump posted that he had authorized a 90-day pause in some higher tariffs while raising the rate for China.
The executive order dated the same day amended the tariff schedule and applied the changes to covered goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern daylight time on April 10.
The reciprocal tariff changes came under different authority from the current investigation.
The written terms tell the company whether its goods fall under the amended tariff schedule and whether its shipment enters before or after the cutoff. The applicable rate can depend on those details and on whether an exemption applies.
After Trump signaled a possible tariff increase on China in October 2025, Bitcoin fell during a broader selloff. That episode shows why a tariff headline can impact crypto investors before importers have any new duties to enter on customs paperwork.
If the USTR determination leads to tariffs, the product coverage, rates, and entry dates will show where costs change and when. Until USTR publishes its findings, the docket remains the place to look for the public decision.

sources.text:
Trump Prepares Aggressive New US Industrial Subsidy Tariffs on China and Europe
The global trade landscape is bracing for a major shockwave as the Trump administration prepares to roll out a sweeping new round of import duties targeting China, the European Union, and more than a dozen other economies. Driven by a months-long investigation into foreign government support for domestic manufacturing, the upcoming tariff package aims to counter what Washington describes as market-distorting industrial overcapacity. US Industrial Subsidy Tariffs
According to reports emerging from Washington, United States Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer could announce the findings of this high-stakes probe as early as this week. While officials caution that the exact rollout timeline remains fluid, the move signals a renewed determination by the White House to use aggressive trade enforcement as its primary economic lever. US Industrial Subsidy Tariffs
The Investigation Behind the New US Industrial Subsidy Tariffs
The foundation for these impending levies is an extensive inquiry conducted by the Office of the US Trade Representative under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act. This statutory authority allows the president to impose unilateral tariffs to counteract unfair foreign trade practices. Initiated in March 2026—shortly after the US Supreme Court invalidated an earlier round of broad global duties in February—the investigation scrutinized 16 major economies, including China, the 27-nation European Union, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam.
At the heart of the administration’s argument is the issue of state-backed industrial subsidies. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has repeatedly asserted that extensive financial and policy support from foreign governments has artificially inflated manufacturing capacity abroad. According to the USTR, this excess capacity enables foreign exporters to flood global markets with artificially cheap goods, systematically undercutting American factories and threatening domestic jobs. US Industrial Subsidy Tariffs
Which Countries and Sectors Face the Brunt of the Levies?
While the White House and the USTR have yet to publish the final tariff schedule, informed sources indicate that the new duties will be tailored to specific economies rather than applied as a flat global rate. The administration intends to align the new measures with the tariff benchmarks President Trump sought to establish in 2025, while respecting existing bilateral trade frameworks.
- China: Beijing is expected to face the steepest penalties. US officials view China’s state subsidies as uniquely pervasive and damaging to global competition. Furthermore, imposing a high rate on Chinese imports allows the administration to push back against domestic criticism that recent diplomatic engagements—including President Trump’s visit to China just last week—were overly lenient. Officials are also weighing a “trigger clause” that would automatically escalate tariffs on China if overcapacity metrics worsen. US Industrial Subsidy Tariffs
- The European Union, Japan, and South Korea: Economies that have already negotiated trade agreements with Washington are expected to receive comparatively moderated treatment. Under the terms of their existing pacts, goods from the EU, Japan, and South Korea are projected to face tariffs capped at 15% or lower.
- India and Vietnam: Both nations are included in the probe and could face higher duty thresholds than European or East Asian allies, depending on how Washington interprets compliance with their respective bilateral trade deals.
In terms of product coverage, the tariffs are expected to apply broadly across most merchandise imported from the targeted nations. However, specific industrial commodities already subject to separate national security tariffs—most notably steel, aluminum, and automobiles—are slated to be excluded from this particular round. US Industrial Subsidy Tariffs
Stacking Duties and Legal Hurdles Ahead
The proposed US industrial subsidy tariffs will not exist in a vacuum; instead, they are designed to stack directly on top of existing trade barriers. In July 2026, the administration implemented tariffs ranging from 10% to 12.5% across roughly 60 economies over allegations that those nations failed to curb forced labor in their supply chains. Layering Section 301 subsidy duties onto those existing penalties will substantially raise the effective import tax on a vast array of consumer and industrial goods entering the United States.
However, the administration’s trade strategy continues to face significant legal and market scrutiny. The July forced-labor tariffs are currently tied up in active litigation before the US Court of International Trade. By anchoring this new November tariff wave in Section 301—a well-established legal mechanism with decades of precedent—the White House aims to insulate the duties from the kind of judicial strike-down that derailed its initial 2025 tariff campaign. US Industrial Subsidy Tariffs
Market Reaction and Global Economic Impact
Financial markets reacted swiftly to news of the impending announcement, with S&P 500 futures dipping 1.25% as investors weighed the potential for renewed inflationary pressures and supply chain disruptions. sources.text:
More than a dozen economies, plus China and the EU, could face higher US tariffs. Nothing is final, but the timing may be today.
China, the European Union and more than a dozen other economies could soon face higher US tariffs. Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, November 24, that the White House is preparing the increase, with an announcement possible as soon as the same day. It rests on a Section 301 investigation into industrial overcapacity, and other outlets have reported on its likely shape. As of this writing, the White House has not formally announced rates, a list of countries or a start date.
That caveat matters more than usual. Outlets don't even agree on the count: some say China, the EU and 14 other economies, while one headline puts it at 15. A White House official reportedly told reporters that any announcement would come directly from the administration and that coverage of it amounts to speculation. Treat every number below as reported, not decided.
The Office of the US Trade Representative opened the probe in March, covering 16 economies including China, the EU, Japan, India, South Korea, Vietnam and Mexico, when it launched in March. It came after the Supreme Court struck down the earlier global tariffs, which had been imposed under emergency powers. Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act is the replacement route, because it lets the administration act on findings of unfair trade practices without going through Congress.
According to the reports carried by The Private Banker and Business Upturn, the EU, Japan and South Korea would face rates of 15% or less. China would get the steepest rate, and Vietnam and India could land higher than the others. Steel, aluminum and autos would be left out, since they already carry separate national-security tariffs.
Class counsel Lawrence Friedman, Elizabeth Cabraser and Nicholas Diamand want the trade court to refund all 330,000 importers that paid IEEPA duties, with interest. Roughly $42 billion or less is still owed, and the Justice Department has until December 9 to respond. - how importers can claim tariff refunds - court case for universal tariff refunds
Frankly, the exclusions tell you more than the headline rates do. The sectors the administration already taxed heavily stay where they are, and everything else, which includes most of what a startup actually imports, is in play.
Why hardware and AI-server builders should pay attention
A Section 301 tariff hits finished goods and components alike, which is exactly where AI infrastructure is exposed. Servers, networking gear, power supplies, cooling parts and circuit boards move through Chinese, Taiwanese, Vietnamese and Mexican factories before they reach a US data center. Mexico was among the economies named in the March probe, and Vietnam is reportedly facing a higher rate than the EU, so the usual escape route of moving final assembly out of China may not be as cheap as it was last year.
The reports don't say how chips themselves will be treated, and that is the open question for anyone selling or buying compute. Earlier Section 301 rounds, from 2018 onward, did carve out some products through exclusion lists, so a carve-out is possible. Don't plan around one until it's published.
If you run a hardware startup with a China-based contract manufacturer, the practical step is dull but urgent: pull your bill of materials, find the customs classification for each line, and work out what a 15% or higher duty does to your unit margin. A company shipping a $400 device with 60% gross margin can absorb a surprise, but one running on 25% cannot. Ask your supplier now whether they will split the cost, because after the proclamation every supplier will be asking the same thing.
Founders without hardware aren't immune. Software companies that sell into Europe could see retaliation aimed at services, and any startup with a China-sourced device in its product, from a point-of-sale tablet to a wearable, faces the same arithmetic.
What to watch next
Three things will settle this. First, whether a White House proclamation or a USTR determination actually appears today, since Bloomberg's timing was a report and not a commitment. Second, the effective date, because a start a few weeks out gives importers time to pull shipments forward. Third, whether the 15% ceiling for allies holds, since the reported rates for Vietnam and India would hurt companies that moved production there to escape China tariffs.
China's response is the other unknown. Beijing has opposed earlier proposed tariff rates and has not commented on this round as far as the reports show. The White House has said nothing on the record about rates, countries or timing.
The USTR has proposed an additional 12.5% tariff on imports from India and many other economies over forced labor enforcement concerns. Trump’s tariff war returns: US prepares fresh duties on India, China and EU
The Trump administration is preparing another round of tariff hikes targeting China, the European Union and 14 other economies, including India. Here's why Washington is considering fresh duties, when they could take effect and what they could mean for Indian exporters and global trade.
New Delhi: Donald Trump’s tariff war appears to be entering another phase. The United States is preparing to raise import duties on China, the European Union (EU) and several other economies, including India, over concerns that government-backed industrial production overseas is hurting American manufacturers. The move could trigger fresh uncertainty across global markets.
According to a report by The Wall Street Journal on November 24, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could announce the findings of a months-long investigation as early as this week. The proposed tariff changes could affect dozens of countries, considering the European Union alone comprises 27 member nations.

Why is the US preparing to raise tariffs again?
On March 11, 2026, Washington launched investigations under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974 to examine excess industrial production across 16 economies.
The Trump administration believes that government subsidies, cheap loans and other forms of financial assistance allow overseas manufacturers to produce goods beyond market demand and sell them at prices that American companies struggle to match.
The investigation covers China, the EU, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India.
How high could the new US tariffs be?
According to The Wall Street Journal, Japan, South Korea and EU members could face tariff rates of 15 per cent or lower. India and Vietnam could face higher rates depending on their respective trade arrangements with Washington.
The final rates, product exemptions and implementation dates are yet to be officially announced.

US tariff hike: What does it mean for India?
India could find itself back at the negotiating table over tariff rates. In February 2026, Washington and New Delhi announced a trade framework that envisaged an 18 per cent reciprocal tariff on Indian goods.
The latest investigation specifically examined India’s manufacturing capacity, including solar modules. Fresh duties could put pressure on Indian exporters across sectors such as textiles, footwear, chemicals, engineering goods and renewable energy equipment, depending on the products covered.
Higher import duties could make Indian products more expensive for American buyers, squeeze exporters’ profit margins and affect employment in export-dependent industries.
What could be the global impact?
Fresh tariffs could increase costs for American businesses, raise consumer prices and disrupt international supply chains. Companies may reconsider sourcing contracts and manufacturing investments. Much will depend on the final tariff rates and whether affected trading partners respond with retaliatory measures.
